title: Lonesome
byline: Dir. Pál Fejős · Universal Pictures · story by Mann Page

evidence.note: Published 1928 by Universal Pictures Corp.; the 95-year US copyright term ran through 31 Dec 2023 and the work entered the public domain on 1 Jan 2024. All works published through 1928 are within the unconditional US PD bright line.
evidence.source: Duke University Center for the Study of the Public Domain — Public Domain Day 2024

evidence.note: Wikimedia Commons explicitly confirms US PD status: 'published (or registered with the U.S. Copyright Office) before January 1, 1931.'

Lonesome is a part-talkie: three dialogue sequences were spliced into the 1928 release after Universal pivoted to sound. Those original 1928 recorded elements—dialogue and any score baked into the period print, including the recurring Irving Berlin composition 'Always' (itself PD, published 1925)—share the film's PD status. However, the 2012 Criterion Collection Blu-ray/DVD restoration includes newly recorded or commissioned musical accompaniment; that recording is an independently copyrighted sound recording. Any reuse should draw from the original 1928 print audio, not a modern accompaniment track found on commercial or streaming copies.

Original story credited to Mann Page, created as a three-page studio outline for Universal in 1928 and never independently published. As a studio-originated work bundled with the film, the story is co-extensive with the film's copyright; it entered the US public domain on 1 Jan 2024 together with the print.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: copying or restoring public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration ADDS can be protected: a newly composed or newly recorded score, colorization, newly written or translated titles and subtitles, and other original additions. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.

The Criterion Collection released Lonesome on Blu-ray and DVD in 2012 (spine #612), including an HD restoration of the hand-tinted color sequences. Criterion's restored master and any accompanying recorded score or packaging materials are independently copyrighted; the disc is not a free source.

editorial:
Pál Fejős's Lonesome (Universal Pictures, 1928) follows two isolated working-class New Yorkers—Jim (Glenn Tryon), a lathe operator, and Mary (Barbara Kent), a telephone switchboard operator—who meet and fall in love during a Fourth of July holiday at Coney Island, only to lose each other in the holiday crowds before discovering they are next-door neighbors. Fejős shot largely on location using a mobile camera, building the film around color tinting, superimposition, and rapid montage rather than conventional narrative continuity; three dialogue sequences were grafted on when Universal pivoted to sound, making Lonesome one of the first part-talkies. The Library of Congress selected it for the National Film Registry in 2010.

The 1928 print is free to reuse: the 95-year US copyright term expired on January 1, 2024, placing Lonesome in the same unconditional public domain category as all US works published through 1928, regardless of whether Universal filed a renewal in the 1950s. The rights trap that actually applies is the Criterion Collection's 2012 Blu-ray and DVD restoration (spine #612). A faithful restoration adds no new copyright to the restored images themselves, but any newly recorded musical accompaniment on the disc is independently protected; ripping the copy-protected disc also risks violating the DMCA's anti-circumvention rules even though the film is public domain. A creator should source from the Internet Archive's copies of the pre-Criterion print and treat any modern audio accompaniment encountered on streaming platforms as protected until the specific license is confirmed.
faq: Is the Lonesome (1928) print in the public domain?

Yes. The 95-year US copyright term for all 1928 publications expired on January 1, 2024, placing the original Universal print in the public domain unconditionally. A faithful restoration adds no new copyright to the restored images themselves, but the Criterion disc may include a newly recorded accompaniment that is independently protected, and ripping the copy-protected disc risks violating the DMCA's anti-circumvention rules.
Can I freely use the dialogue or music from this film?

The original 1928 recorded sound elements—three dialogue scenes and any score or music baked into the period print, including Irving Berlin's 'Always' (itself PD, published 1925)—are public domain along with the film. If you are working from a modern restoration copy sourced from Criterion or a streaming platform, the audio track may include a separately copyrighted recorded accompaniment. Source from the Internet Archive's original-print copies to stay clearly within public domain.
